blocks.text:
Design an ATM that lets a customer insert a card, authenticate with a PIN, and then withdraw cash, deposit money, or check their balance. The machine must verify every transaction with the bank, dispense the right mix of notes, return the card, and stay correct even when things fail midway.

The ATM is a physical machine wrapped around two hard problems: a session that moves through strict stages (no card, card inserted, authenticated, dispensing), and money movement that must never be wrong, even on power failure or a network drop. The first is a classic fit for the State pattern; the second forces careful ordering of checks, debits, and dispensing.

  • Actors: the customer at the machine, the bank service behind it, and the operator who refills cash
  • Scope: one machine, card and PIN authentication, withdraw, deposit, and balance inquiry, with an in memory bank stub behind an interface
  • Goal: a clean object oriented design where every rupee is accounted for on every path

The ATM is a state machine standing between a person and their money. The design is judged on what happens when things go wrong.
These are the behaviours the ATM must support for customers and operators. Everything else in the design exists to deliver this list safely.

metadata.alt: Functional requirements at a glance: authenticate, transact, dispense, and always return the card

items: Insert card: read the card and start a session
Authenticate: verify the PIN with the bank, allowing at most three attempts
Withdraw: validate the amount, confirm notes are available, debit the bank, and dispense
Deposit: accept cash or cheque and credit the account
Balance inquiry: show the current account balance
Dispense correct notes: break the amount into available denominations
Cancel and eject: the customer can abort at any point and always gets the card back
Operator: refill note cassettes and audit the cash held

blocks.text: An ATM is held to a higher bar than most systems because it hands out physical money. Five qualities dominate the design.

metadata.alt: The five non-functional pillars for an ATM

blocks.text: PINs are verified by the bank, never stored on the machine, and three failures retain the card. Sessions end with the card ejected and state cleared.
The account debit and the cash dispense must effectively be one atomic outcome. The design orders checks so a debit never happens unless dispensing is guaranteed possible, and failures roll back.
New transaction types, new note denominations, and new authentication methods must be added as new classes, not edits to the tested core.
If the bank link is down the machine fails safely: it refuses transactions cleanly and returns the card rather than hanging a session.
One customer uses the keypad, but the same account is reachable from other channels at the same time, so all balance changes go through an atomic, bank side debit.
Confirm the scope before designing, because ATM can mean anything from a cash dispenser to a full banking kiosk. These are the questions worth asking.

items: Transactions: withdraw only, or also deposit, balance inquiry, and PIN change?
Denominations: which notes does the machine hold, and is the amount restricted to multiples of the smallest note?
PIN policy: how many attempts, and is the card retained or returned after the last failure?
Limits: is there a per transaction or daily withdrawal limit?
Bank connectivity: is the bank always online, and who is the source of truth for balances?
Accounts: one account per card, or can a card select between accounts?
Receipts: are printed receipts in scope?

blocks.text: Assumed answers for this design: withdraw, deposit, and balance inquiry; notes of 2000, 500, and 100 with amounts in multiples of 100; three PIN attempts then the card is retained; a daily limit enforced by the bank; the bank is authoritative and reachable; one account per card; receipts noted as an extension.
These decisions keep the design honest and the interview scoped. Say them out loud so the interviewer can redirect early.

items: Money: whole rupees as long integers, no floating point anywhere
Amounts: withdrawals must be multiples of 100, the smallest note
Authority: the bank service owns balances and limits; the ATM never computes a balance itself
Session: one customer session at a time, ended by eject, retain, or timeout
Cash: the machine tracks note counts per denomination in cassettes
Ordering: notes are reserved before the debit, and the debit happens before dispensing
State: in memory for the interview; the database section shows the persistent schema

blocks.text: Underline the nouns in the requirements and the classes name themselves. Each entity below owns exactly one responsibility.

metadata.alt: The core entities and how they connect

items: ATM: the context object owning the session, the current card, and the current state
ATMState: an interface with one implementation per session stage: Idle, CardInserted, Authenticated, Dispensing
Card: the card data read at insertion: number, linked account, expiry
BankService: the interface to the bank: verify PIN, get balance, debit, credit
Account: the bank side record holding balance and daily usage
CashDispenser: owns the note cassettes and turns an amount into physical notes
NoteHandler chain: one handler per denomination, linked 2000 to 500 to 100
Transaction: a record of each attempted operation for auditing

blocks.text: Naming the relationship types shows you know who owns whom. The four classic relationships all appear in this design.

metadata.alt: Composition, aggregation, association, and inheritance in the ATM

items: ATM composes CashDispenser: the dispenser is part of the machine and dies with it
CashDispenser composes its cassette counts: note inventory has no life outside the dispenser
ATM aggregates the current Card: the card exists independently and leaves with the customer
CashDispenser aggregates the NoteHandler chain: handlers are assembled outside and linked together
ATM uses BankService: it calls the bank but owns nothing inside it
States call back into the ATM: to read the card, reach the bank, and switch states
IdleState, CardInsertedState, AuthenticatedState, DispensingState implement ATMState
Note2000Handler, Note500Handler, Note100Handler extend the abstract NoteHandler

blocks.text: The class diagram captures the whole design in one view: the ATM delegates to its state, composes the cash dispenser with its handler chain, and talks to the bank through an interface.

metadata.alt: UML class diagram of the ATM system

blocks.text: Reading guide: dashed triangle arrows are interface realisation, solid triangles are inheritance, the filled diamond is composition, and open diamonds are aggregation. The two hierarchies, states on the left and note handlers on the right, are the two patterns at work.
Two patterns carry this design, with two more in supporting roles. Name each with its justification, never as a buzzword.
Why needed: the same button means different things at different moments. Entering a PIN before a card is inserted is meaningless; withdrawing before authentication must be impossible.

Why it is the best choice: the alternative is flags like cardInserted and pinVerified checked in every method, which grows into unreadable, bug prone branching. One class per stage makes the legal transitions explicit.
What it solves: illegal operations are rejected by construction, and adding a stage, like a language selection screen, is one new class.

metadata.alt: The session states and the actions that move between them

blocks.text: Why needed: breaking 3500 into notes is a cascading decision: the 2000 cassette takes its share, passes the remainder to the 500 cassette, which passes on to the 100 cassette.

Why it is the best choice: each handler owns one denomination and its count, and the chain order encodes the dispensing policy. Adding a 200 note is one new handler linked in, with zero edits elsewhere.
What it solves: no monolithic note calculation, per cassette accounting for free, and a clean failure when the chain cannot cover the amount.

metadata.alt: The handler chain breaks 3500 into one 2000 note and three 500 notes

blocks.text: The ATM class is a facade: the keypad and screen call five simple methods and never orchestrate the bank, dispenser, and states themselves. A single machine instance can be enforced with a singleton, but say the tradeoff: dependency injection of one instance tests better.
State runs the session, Chain of Responsibility counts the notes. Everything else is glue.
blocks.content: State runs the session, Chain of Responsibility counts the notes. Everything else is glue.

blocks.text: For every class: its single responsibility, its attributes, and its methods. Keep each one small enough to read in a minute.

items: Responsibility: own the session context and delegate every action to the current state
Attributes: state, currentCard, bankService, cashDispenser
Methods: insertCard(card), enterPin(pin), withdraw(amount), checkBalance(), ejectCard(), plus operator refillNotes
IdleState: accepts only insertCard, which stores the card and moves to CardInserted
CardInsertedState: accepts enterPin, counting attempts; three failures retain the card and reset
AuthenticatedState: accepts withdraw, deposit, and balance inquiry; validates then moves to Dispensing for cash
DispensingState: releases notes, records the transaction, ejects the card, and resets to Idle
Card responsibility: immutable data read from the card: number, accountId, expiry
Account responsibility: bank side record with balance and dailyUsed; mutated only by the bank service
Responsibility: the single authority for authentication and money: verifyPin, getBalance, debit, credit
Attributes: account store in the stub; a network client in production
Methods: all validation of balance and daily limits happens here, atomically
CashDispenser responsibility: answer canDispense(amount) and perform dispense(amount) through the chain
NoteHandler responsibility: one denomination cassette: its note value, its count, and a link to the next handler
Methods: plan(amount) computes the note split without committing; dispense(amount) commits it

blocks.text: Three abstractions carry the volatility of this system: the session stage, the bank behind the wire, and the note cassettes.
Why ATMState is an interface: the machine must hold any stage through one type, and every stage answers the same actions, even when the answer is a rejection.

Why BankService is an interface: the interview uses an in memory stub, production uses a network client, and tests use a mock. The ATM cannot tell the difference, which is exactly the point of depending on an abstraction.
Three workflows define this machine: a successful withdrawal, a failed authentication, and a withdrawal the machine itself cannot serve.

metadata.alt: Sequence diagram of a successful cash withdrawal

blocks.text: The state checks the notes before asking the bank to debit, so a successful debit is always followed by a successful dispense. That ordering is the heart of the money safety argument.

metadata.alt: Sequence diagram of failed PIN attempts

blocks.text: Each failure is counted by the CardInserted state. The third failure retains the card and resets to Idle, which protects the account from guessing attacks.
12.3 Failure path: ATM out of cash
blocks.content: 12.3 Failure path: ATM out of cash

metadata.alt: Sequence diagram of a withdrawal the machine cannot serve

blocks.text: Because the cash check runs first, the bank is never called and no debit happens. The customer keeps their money and their card, and the machine stays consistent.
The withdrawal flow is a corridor of gates: amount validity, machine cash, then bank approval. A request only moves forward after passing each gate.

metadata.alt: The withdrawal flow with its three validation gates

items: The customer inserts a card; the machine reads it and moves to CardInserted
The customer enters the PIN; the bank verifies it and the machine moves to Authenticated
The customer requests 3500; the amount is a valid multiple and within limits
The dispenser confirms it can cover 3500 with current notes and reserves them
The bank debits the account atomically, checking balance and daily limit
The dispenser releases one 2000 and three 500 notes
The transaction is recorded, the card is ejected, and the machine returns to Idle
Wrong PIN: attempt counted, session continues until the third failure retains the card
Invalid amount: rejected instantly, no state change, no bank call
Machine short of notes: rejected before any debit, balance untouched
Bank declines: reserved notes are released and the customer sees the reason
Dispense hardware jams after debit: the transaction is flagged for automatic reversal, the one case needing recovery

blocks.text: The customer surface is five methods, all delegated to the current state. Operators get two more.

metadata.alt: The public API surface for customers and operators

codes.python:
# customer facing
def insert_card(self, card: Card) -> None: ...      # start a session
def enter_pin(self, pin: str) -> None: ...           # authenticate, max 3 attempts
def withdraw(self, amount: int) -> None: ...         # validate, debit, dispense
def check_balance(self) -> int: ...                  # read from the bank
def eject_card(self) -> None: ...                    # cancel or finish, always returns the card

# operator facing
def refill_notes(self, note_value: int, count: int) -> None: ...
def audit_cash(self) -> Dict[int, int]: ...

items: insertCard: legal only in Idle; every other state rejects a second card
enterPin: legal only in CardInserted; counts attempts internally
withdraw and checkBalance: legal only in Authenticated
ejectCard: legal in every state except Idle, so the customer is never trapped

blocks.text: Every failure gets a specific exception, and every exception leaves the machine consistent. Money is refunded or never taken, and the card is always accounted for.

metadata.alt: The failure categories and their exceptions

items: InvalidAmountException: not a multiple of 100, zero, or negative
InvalidPinFormatException: malformed PIN rejected before reaching the bank
InsufficientCashException: the chain cannot cover the amount; raised before any debit
BankUnavailableException: the network is down; the session ends safely with the card returned
InvalidPinException: wrong PIN with the remaining attempt count
CardBlockedException and CardExpiredException: rejected at insertion
InsufficientBalanceException and DailyLimitExceededException: raised by the bank during the atomic debit
DispenseFailureException: hardware jam after a debit triggers an automatic reversal request
Every handler guarantees: no path leaves a debit without cash or cash without a debit unflagged

blocks.text: The dangerous race is not at the keypad, it is at the account. The same balance is reachable from this ATM, other ATMs, and online banking at the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two channels racing on one account: the atomic conditional debit lets exactly one win

items: Account race: two withdrawals read balance 5000 and both try to take 4000
Cassette race: in a multi dispenser design, two requests counting the same notes
Session race: a timeout firing while a withdrawal is mid flight

blocks.text: The debit must be a single atomic conditional operation at the bank: subtract if and only if balance and daily limit allow. The ATM never does read, decide, write on a balance.

In a real bank this is a conditional update inside a database transaction, but the invariant is identical: the check and the change are one indivisible step per account. Note counts on the machine use the same rule inside the dispenser.
Every likely change lands as a new class, not an edit. That is the payoff for the two pattern backbone.

metadata.alt: Extensions plug into existing abstractions without edits

items: New denomination: one new NoteHandler linked into the chain
New transaction type, like mini statements or PIN change: a new operation on the Authenticated state, or a Transaction hierarchy if they multiply
Cardless withdrawal: a new authentication path producing the same Authenticated state
Receipt printer and notifications: observers on transaction events
Multi account cards: an account selection stage, which is one new state

blocks.text: Future enhancements: contactless cards, biometric authentication, and cheque scanning all attach at the authentication boundary or as new states, leaving the money path untouched.
The structure earns SOLID rather than declaring it. Here is the mapping, principle by principle.

metadata.alt: How the ATM design maps to SOLID

items: Single Responsibility: states run the session, the dispenser moves cash, the bank owns balances, the ATM only coordinates
Open Closed: new notes, new transactions, and new auth methods are new classes; the withdrawal corridor never changes
Liskov Substitution: any ATMState drops in wherever State is expected; the machine cannot tell stages apart
Interface Segregation: ATMState and BankService stay small; the keypad sees only five methods
Dependency Inversion: the ATM depends on BankService and ATMState abstractions, with the stub, client, or mock injected

blocks.text: ATM interviews are won on the ugly cases. Each of these has a defined answer in this design.

metadata.alt: The edge cases the design must survive

items: Amount not payable with current notes: canDispense fails even though the amount is valid, and no debit happens
Power failure mid dispense: the journal records debit and dispense separately; recovery reverses unmatched debits
Card left behind: a timeout retracts the card and ends the session
Daily limit reached: the bank rejects the debit atomically with a specific error
Expired or blocked card: rejected at insertion, before a PIN is ever requested
Cancel mid transaction: ejectCard works in every non idle state and releases any reserved notes
Deposit envelope without amount confirmation: credited only after operator verification, noted as policy

blocks.text: Every customer operation is constant time. Nothing scales with the number of accounts or past transactions on the machine side.

items: insertCard, enterPin, checkBalance: O(1) plus one bank round trip
withdraw: O(k) over k denominations for the note plan, k is 3, effectively O(1), plus one bank call
refillNotes and auditCash: O(k) map updates and reads
O(k) for the note cassettes over k denominations
O(1) per session: one card, one state, one pending amount
O(T) only in the persistent journal of T transactions, which lives in the database

blocks.text: The persistent truth of an ATM is its transaction journal. Cards and accounts live with the bank; the machine persists its cash state and every attempted operation.

metadata.alt: Entity relationship diagram for the ATM persistent data

items: CARD: card records with status, owned by the bank
ACCOUNT: balances and daily usage, the single source of truth
ATM_TXN: one row per attempted operation with type, amount, and status, the audit trail
ATM_CASH: live note counts per denomination for this machine
ATM_TXN(account_id, created_at): statement queries and daily limit checks
ATM_TXN(status): the reversal job scans pending and failed rows
CARD(account_id): card lookups during support flows

blocks.text: The exit rule from the workflows applies here: debit, journal row, and cash count change commit together, so recovery after a crash can always tell what physically happened.
Strong candidates finish by opening doors, not closing them. These are the natural follow ups.

items: Note planning: prefer emptying overfull cassettes to balance stock, a pluggable chain ordering
Offline PIN verification: chip based local verification when the bank link is briefly down, with tight limits
Predictive refill: use the journal to forecast when cash runs out
Reversal flow: how a debit without a dispense is detected and refunded automatically
State versus flags: why four state classes beat three booleans, argued with the wrong PIN flow
Chain versus a greedy loop: the loop is fine for fixed notes; the chain wins when cassettes own counts and policies
Idempotency: every debit carries a transaction id, so a retried request never double debits
Fleet management: thousands of ATMs report cash and faults to a central service; each machine remains autonomous
Reconciliation: the bank matches journal rows to ledger entries nightly and flags mismatches

blocks.text: The full Java implementation in dependency order: data classes, the bank, the dispenser chain, the states, and the ATM facade with a runnable demo.

codes.python:
class ATM:
    def __init__(self, bank: "BankService", dispenser: "CashDispenser"):
        self._state: ATMState = IdleState()
        self._bank = bank
        self._dispenser = dispenser
        self._card: Optional[Card] = None
        self._pending_amount = 0

    # customer facing, all delegated to the current state
    def insert_card(self, c: "Card") -> None: self._state.insert_card(self, c)
    def enter_pin(self, pin: str) -> None: self._state.enter_pin(self, pin)
    def withdraw(self, amount: int) -> None: self._state.withdraw(self, amount)
    def check_balance(self) -> None: self._state.check_balance(self)
    def eject_card(self) -> None: self._state.eject_card(self)
    def dispense(self) -> None: self._state.eject_card(self)          # DispensingState completes here

    # callbacks used by states
    def set_state(self, s: ATMState) -> None: self._state = s
    def set_card(self, c: "Card") -> None: self._card = c
    def get_card(self) -> "Card": return self._card
    def get_bank(self) -> "BankService": return self._bank
    def get_dispenser(self) -> "CashDispenser": return self._dispenser
    def set_pending_amount(self, a: int) -> None: self._pending_amount = a
    def get_pending_amount(self) -> int: return self._pending_amount
    def return_card(self) -> None:
        self.display("Card returned")
        self._card = None
        self._pending_amount = 0
    def retain_card(self) -> None:
        self.display("Card retained")
        self._card = None
        self._pending_amount = 0
    def display(self, msg: str) -> None: print(msg)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    bank = InMemoryBankService()
    bank.add_account(Account("ACC-1", 10_000), "CARD-1", "1234")

    chain = Note2000Handler(10)
    chain.link_next(Note500Handler(20)).link_next(Note100Handler(50))
    atm = ATM(bank, CashDispenser(chain))

    card = Card("CARD-1", "ACC-1", date.today() + timedelta(days=730))
    atm.insert_card(card)         # Idle -> CardInserted
    atm.enter_pin("1234")         # CardInserted -> Authenticated
    atm.withdraw(3500)            # cash check, debit, Dispensing -> Idle
    # prints: Dispensed: {2000: 1, 500: 3}, Card returned

blocks.text: This is the walkthrough that scores, in order. Lead with the two patterns and the money ordering.

items: Open by naming the two backbones: State for the session, Chain of Responsibility for the notes
Draw the state diagram early: Idle, CardInserted, Authenticated, Dispensing, with the three PIN attempt rule
Stress the money ordering: validate amount, check cash, then debit, then dispense, and why that order
Show the note chain on 3500: one 2000, three 500, and what happens when a cassette is empty
Point out that the bank owns balances and the debit is one atomic conditional step
Cover the power failure case: the journal plus reversal is the answer interviewers wait for
Explain plan versus commit in the dispenser: never deduct notes you might not hand over
Close with extensibility: a new note or a new transaction type is one new class

blocks.text: Every choice here has a defensible alternative. Knowing both sides is what separates memorisation from design.
26.1 Chain of Responsibility versus a greedy loop
blocks.content: 26.1 Chain of Responsibility versus a greedy loop

blocks.text: A simple loop over denominations computes the same split in five lines. The chain earns its place when each cassette owns its count, its refill, and its policy; the loop wins on pure simplicity. Say the tradeoff and pick the chain here because cassettes are real stateful hardware.
26.2 Debit before dispense versus dispense before debit
blocks.content: 26.2 Debit before dispense versus dispense before debit

blocks.text: Debit first risks a jam after taking money; dispense first risks giving cash without payment. Debit first with automatic reversal is the industry answer, because a reversal wrongs no one, while unpaid cash is unrecoverable.
26.3 State classes versus an enum switch
blocks.content: 26.3 State classes versus an enum switch

blocks.text: An enum with a switch per action is compact for four states, but the PIN attempt counter shows why classes win: CardInsertedState carries its own attempts field naturally, where the enum needs external bookkeeping.
26.4 ATM side versus bank side validation
blocks.content: 26.4 ATM side versus bank side validation

blocks.text: The ATM could pre check balances to fail fast, but the bank must recheck atomically anyway. Doing validation only at the bank keeps one source of truth and avoids double maintenance of rules like daily limits.
One machine is naturally a singleton, but injecting the single instance keeps tests clean and lets a simulator run many machines side by side. Prefer injection and mention the singleton temptation.
Real ATMs are audited machines with decades of hard lessons. These are the practices that carry from this design into production.

items: Electronic journal: every step, card in, PIN result, debit, dispense, is journaled locally before it happens, enabling exact recovery
Automatic reversal: a debit without a matching dispense confirmation is reversed by a reconciliation job
Idempotent debits: each transaction carries a unique id so network retries never double charge
PIN security: PIN blocks are encrypted at the keypad by hardware and never touch application memory in plain text
Cash reconciliation: counted notes at refill must match the journal, with alerts on drift
Monitoring: cash levels, dispense failures, and decline rates on dashboards, with predictive refill alerts
